title: Are internet videos useful sources of information during global public health emergencies? A case study of YouTube videos during the 2015-16 Zika virus pandemic
screen_reason: Content analysis of 101 YouTube videos retrieved with the query 'zika virus' (search date 1 December 2016). Each video was watched in full by two researchers and classified against current scientific evidence as informative, misleading or personal experience: 24/101 (23.8%, 95% CI 16.5-32.9) were misleading, i.e. contained erroneous and/or scientifically unproven information. That is a share of items judged for veracity against an external ground truth, with a stated denominator - a CONTENT estimate. The DISCERN and GQS scores in the same paper are quality instruments and are not used for prevalence.

estimates.country: Not stated (global YouTube search; English-language videos; uploaders include CNN, BBC, WHO, CDC, White House and independent users)
estimates.date: Search executed 1 December 2016; videos had been online 186-486 days (uploads roughly August 2015 - June 2016)
estimates.measure_type: % of retrieved YouTube 'zika virus' videos classified as misleading (erroneous and/or scientifically unproven content)
estimates.denominator: 101 YouTube videos analysed - the first 120 results (6 pages) for the query 'zika virus' sorted by relevance on 1 Dec 2016, minus 19 excluded (5 duplicates, 10 non-English, 4 with viewer-interaction features disabled)
estimates.definition: "if the video contained erroneous and/or scientifically unproven information about ZIKV (based on currently available scientific evidence), it was marked as misleading"
estimates.misinfo_def: No standalone definition of misinformation; the operational rule is the classification rule itself - informative = 'scientifically correct and accurate information about ZIKV'; misleading = 'erroneous and/or scientifically unproven information about ZIKV (based on currently available scientific evidence)'; a third, non-overlapping category was personal-experience videos.
estimates.source_quote: Results: Overall, 70.3% videos were informative, while 23.8% and 5.9% videos were mislead- ing and related to personal experiences, respectively.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract, Results (p. 320); the same figures appear in Results and observations (p. 323) and in Table 1 ('Video type: Informative 71, 70.3 (60.8-78.3); Misleading 24, 23.8 (16.5-32.9); Personal experience 6, 5.9 (2.8-12.4)')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: "all the selected videos were viewed in their entirety independently by two researchers" and judged against currently available scientific evidence; "There was 100% concordance between the two researchers while carrying out this classification." Reliability (DISCERN-adapted, 5 items) and quality (GQS) were scored separately by two reviewers with the final score assigned by consensus.
estimates.moderator_quote: A search for ZIKV related videos in YouTube ... on 1 December 2016 using the query term 'zika virus' returned approximately 705,000 results. ... the first 120 videos (i.e. initial 6 pages of the search results, with 20 videos listed per page) were screened for the study. The videos were sorted by relevance (i.e. the default filter setting in YouTube) during this process.
estimates.notes: Clean, verbatim count and percentage with a CI. denom_selection=curated because the denominator is rank-truncated (first 6 pages of relevance-sorted results out of ~705,000 hits); the authors deliberately used relevance rather than view-count or date sorting to avoid a more biased set, and note themselves that even a relevance-sorted list contains a sizeable share of misleading videos. denom_scope=topical (single-issue 'zika virus' keyword corpus). The three categories are mutually exclusive and exhaustive (70.3 + 23.8 + 5.9 = 100). Note that 'misleading' here includes 'scientifically unproven' content, which is broader than demonstrably false - hence breadth=misleading. Country is Global: an unrestricted YouTube search executed from India, non-English videos excluded, uploaders international. topic=health_other (Zika, an emerging infectious disease; not covid19 and not vaccines). QUOTE NOTE: source_quote is taken from the abstract because the body text is rendered as interleaved columns; the hyphen-space in 'mislead- ing' is the printed line break. The body sentence is 'Altogether, 71 videos (70.3%, 95% CI: 60.8 - 70.3%) were deemed informative; whereas 24 videos (23.8%, 95% CI: 16.5 - 32.9%) were categorized as misleading (Table 1)'; note the paper miswrites the informative CI as 60.8-70.3 in the body while Table 1 gives 60.8-78.3.

missed_or_uncertain: (a) NO exposure/view-share row is derivable. The 101 videos drew 8,769,304 views in total and misleading videos were more viewed than informative ones (median 30,632 vs 16,176, p = 0.054), liked, shared and commented on more, but the paper reports only MEDIANS for the informative/misleading comparison (Table 3), never the total views accruing to the 24 misleading videos. The only total-view breakdown (Table 5) is by upload source WITHIN the 71 informative videos, so it cannot yield a misinformation exposure share. This is the single most valuable number the paper fails to report. (b) QUALITY measures not turned into rows (they would be QUALITY construct, excluded from prevalence, and any threshold is arbitrary): GQS distribution 24 (23.76%) scored 1, 34 (33.66%) scored 2, 25 (24.75%) scored 3, 14 (13.86%) scored 4, 4 (3.96%) scored 5, median 2; DISCERN-adapted reliability 18 (17.82%) scored 0 and 6 (5.94%) scored 5, median 2; the summary claim 'more than 50% videos were of poor quality' is a cross-category sum (23.76 + 33.66) and is barred by R8 anyway. (c) Content-coverage shares (59.41% covered epidemiology, 63.37% clinical features, 40.59% prevention/management, 13.86% none of the three) are completeness, not veracity. (d) Source distribution and the odds ratios (independent users 6.48 times more likely to post misleading videos, 95% CI 1.69-24.83) are associations, not prevalence; the underlying 2x2 cells in Table 2 (e.g. 14/31 = 45.16% of independent-user videos misleading, 7/40 = 17.5% of news-agency videos misleading) are verbatim sub-shares I chose not to extract as separate rows under R4 - they are source subgroups of the same corpus, not the paper's headline, but an adjudicator wanting a source-level moderator could take them from Table 2. (e) The discussion's comparison figures from other studies (16.2% H1N1, 20.7% West Nile, 33% hypertension, etc.) are cited from elsewhere and barred by R8.

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis. Single query ('zika virus') run once, on 1 December 2016, returning ~705,000 results; the first 120 relevance-sorted videos were screened, with the authors explicitly justifying relevance-sorting over view-count or date sorting to limit selection/coverage bias. Exclusions: 5 duplicated in part or whole, 10 non-English, 4 with viewer-interaction features disabled - leaving N = 101. Video type classified by two researchers who watched every video in full, independently, with 100% concordance; DISCERN-adapted reliability (5 yes/no items, 0-5) and GQS quality (1-5) scored by two reviewers with consensus adjudication. Viewer metrics (views, likes, dislikes, shares, comments) recorded on the same day for every video, so the popularity data are a single-day snapshot. Analysis: counts with 95% CIs, medians with ranges, Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis, crude and adjusted logistic regression (adjusted for views, shares, video length), SPSS 22, two-sided alpha 0.05. Main limitations for prevalence use: rank-truncated, single-day, single-query, English-only sample of one platform; no sensitivity analysis for the excluded 19 videos; and no reporting of how views distribute across misleading vs informative videos.
rob.item6_quote: If the video contained scientifically correct and accurate information about ZIKV, it was marked as informative or useful. On the other hand, if the video contained erroneous and/or scientifically unproven information about ZIKV (based on currently available scientific evidence), it was marked as misleading.
rob.item10_quote: Altogether, 71 videos (70.3%, 95% CI: 60.8 - 70.3%) were deemed informative; whereas 24 videos (23.8%, 95% CI: 16.5 - 32.9%) were categorized as misleading.
